lead: Time division multiplexing (TDM) lets many signals share one link by giving each signal a repeating slice of time called a slot. All signals use the full bandwidth of the link, but only one signal uses it at a time. A receiver knows the slot order from a frame marker, so it can separate the samples. Telephone trunks, digital exchanges and PCM systems use TDM. In India an E1 line at 2.048 Mbit/s carries 32 such slots, enough for 30 speech calls plus signalling and synchronisation.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for the sampling rate, Chapter 4.2 for PAM, and Chapter 4.4 for PCM code words.

sections.h3: Frame, slot and the TDM idea

blocks.text: TDM is time sharing. One frame is one complete round of all channels. Its duration is Tf = 1/fs, where Tf is the frame duration in seconds and fs is the sampling rate in samples per second. For a 4 kHz voice signal sampled at 8 kHz, Tf = 125 μs.

Inside the frame each channel gets a slot. In PCM the slot carries the n-bit code word of one sample. A guard time is a small idle gap between slots; it absorbs timing error at the cost of some capacity. A synchronisation bit or word marks the start of the frame.

Each input is called a channel. For N equal channels the frame has N data slots plus sync. The figure shows four 8-bit channel slots and one sync bit in a 125 μs frame. The order repeats every frame. The frame rate equals f<sub>s</sub>, not the bit rate. If one bit lasts T<sub>b</sub> seconds, an n-bit slot lasts nT<sub>b</sub> seconds, plus any guard time.

sections.h3: PAM, PCM and the bit rate

blocks.text: With PAM, each slot holds one analog sample. The multiplexer samples channel 1, then channel 2, and so on; the receiver uses a sample-and-hold circuit to stretch each sample. With PCM, each quantised sample becomes an n-bit code word. The multiplexer can interleave whole words, so a channel's n bits stay together, or interleave bit by bit, so the bits of one word are spread over n rounds and must be reassembled.

blocks.where: R<sub>b</sub> is the multiplexed bit rate in bit/s; N is the number of data channels; n is the number of bits per sample per channel; S is the number of synchronisation and signalling bits per frame; f<sub>s</sub> is the frame rate in frames/s.

blocks.text: E1 is a standard example: 8 kHz frames, 32 slots, 8 bits per slot. R<sub>b</sub> = 32 × 8 × 8000 = 2.048 Mbit/s. Thirty slots carry speech, slot 0 carries framing and alarms, and slot 16 carries signalling.
TDM is the multiplexing idea. TDMA is multiple access, where users take turns on a shared radio channel. Some syllabi write TDMA for that access method.

The receiver must know where each frame and slot starts. A single sync bit per frame is a weak marker, because a data bit in the same position can look like sync. Many systems therefore use a longer sync word, sent every frame or spread over a multiframe, to avoid false locking. The clock is recovered from transitions in the received line signal; line coding is covered in Chapter 4.8.

Timing error causes cross-talk. If the receiver samples early, it may read the tail of the previous slot; if it samples late, it may read the start of the next slot. Guard time reduces this. If sync is lost, the receiver may slip by one slot and route channel 1 into channel 2; this is a slot slip (loss of frame alignment). A frame slip is the loss or repetition of a whole frame when the receiver clock drifts.

TDM shares time, not frequency. FDM, covered in Unit 2, gives each signal a band of frequencies for all time. TDM gives each signal the full band for a short slot. The receiver's clock must match the transmitter's clock closely; small drift is corrected by the sync pattern. Large drift cannot be corrected and causes errors.

figure.caption: A 125 µs frame carries four 8-bit channel slots and one synchronisation bit; each 8-bit slot lasts 30.3 µs and the sync bit lasts 3.8 µs.

spec.aria: One 125 microsecond frame carries four 8-bit channel slots followed by one synchronisation bit, giving 33 bits per frame.

examples.question: Four 4 kHz signals are sampled at 8 kHz and coded with 8-bit PCM. One synchronisation bit is added per frame. Find the frame duration, bits per frame, and bit rate.
steps: The sampling rate is f<sub>s</sub> = 8 kHz, so T<sub>f</sub> = 1/f<sub>s</sub> = 1/8000 s = 125 μs.
Each channel sends one 8-bit word per frame. Data bits = 4 × 8 = 32 bits.
Add one sync bit: total bits per frame = 32 + 1 = 33 bits.
R<sub>b</sub> = total bits / T<sub>f</sub> = 33 / 125 μs = 264,000 bit/s = 264 kbit/s. Equivalently R<sub>b</sub> = (4×8 + 1) × 8000 = 264 kbit/s.
One bit lasts 125 μs / 33 = 3.79 μs, so an 8-bit slot lasts 30.3 μs.
examples.answer: T<sub>f</sub> = 125 μs, 33 bits per frame (32 data plus 1 sync), and R<sub>b</sub> = 264 kbit/s.
examples.check:
fs = 8000
Tf_us = (1/fs) * 1e6
data_bits = 4 * 8
total_bits = data_bits + 1
Rb_kbps = total_bits / (Tf_us * 1e-6) / 1000
print(Tf_us)
print(data_bits)
print(total_bits)
print(Rb_kbps)

traps: Frame rate is f<sub>s</sub>, not R<sub>b</sub>. A 264 kbit/s stream with 33 bits per frame still has 8000 frames/s.
Do not forget sync bits, alarm bits or a signalling slot. Use (N n + S) f<sub>s</sub>, not N n f<sub>s</sub>.
TDM shares time; FDM shares frequency. TDMA is multiple access, not the same word as TDM.
Slot duration and bit duration differ. In the example an 8-bit slot is 30.3 μs, while one bit is 3.79 μs.
Keep units: 125 μs = 125 × 10⁻⁶ s (or 125 × 10<sup>-6</sup> s); 264,000 bit/s = 264 kbit/s = 0.264 Mbit/s.

quiz.q: Define frame and slot in TDM.
quiz.a: A frame is one complete round of all channels. A slot is the time position assigned to one channel inside the frame.

quiz.q: Why is a guard time used between TDM slots?
quiz.a: It absorbs small timing errors so a receiver does not read a neighbouring slot. It costs some capacity because no data is sent during the gap.

quiz.q: Six 3.4 kHz channels are sampled at 8 kHz, coded with 7-bit PCM, and 2 sync bits are added per frame. Find R<sub>b</sub>.
quiz.a: Bits per frame = 6×7 + 2 = 44. R<sub>b</sub> = 44 × 8000 = 352,000 bit/s = 352 kbit/s.

quiz.q: A TDM receiver's clock runs slightly fast. Explain how cross-talk can appear.
quiz.a: The receiver samples earlier than the true slot centre. If the drift exceeds the guard time, it reads part of the previous slot, so one channel's sample leaks into another.

quiz.q: An E1 frame has 32 slots, 8 bits per slot, and a frame rate of 8 kHz. Find R<sub>b</sub>.
Distinguish word interleaving from bit interleaving.
quiz.a: Word interleaving keeps the n bits of one code word together in a slot. Bit interleaving sends one bit per channel in turn, so the receiver must reassemble each word.

quiz.q: Why is a sync word often used instead of a single sync bit?
quiz.a: A single bit can match a data bit and cause false locking. A longer word makes false detection unlikely, at the cost of extra bits per frame.

quiz.q: State the difference between TDM and TDMA.
quiz.a: TDM multiplexes channels onto one link. TDMA is a multiple-access method in which users take turns on a shared medium.

beyond: Not for the exam. E1/T1 frames grew into SDH/SONET and optical transport networks, where time slots are carried inside much larger frames. Packet networks replaced strict TDM for data, but TDM thinking survives in time-sensitive networking and industrial Ethernet schedules. 5G uses OFDM with time-frequency resource blocks, which is a cousin of TDM. Search next for E1 frame structure, TDM synchronisation, and time-sensitive networking scheduling.
